homes.title: Converting a newer home: what to check first
homes.intro: On a modern estate house, two things are worth establishing early, and a good builder raises them rather than leaving you to find out later.
homes.body: The first is restrictive covenants. These are private legal conditions written into a property's title deeds, entirely separate from planning permission, and modern developments sometimes include them, occasionally restricting alterations, or requiring consent from the developer or a management company before you make changes. They will not show up in a planning search, so the place to check is your deeds, and if there is any doubt your solicitor or conveyancer is the person to confirm the position. It is not usually a barrier, but it is far better known about at the start than discovered halfway through.
homes.closing: The second is the roof. Newer houses often have trussed roofs, prefabricated frames that fill the loft with bracing, which can still be converted but need the trusses reworked and new structural support added, so it is a bigger job than on an older cut roof. Some modern homes also have shallow, low-pitch roofs that limit what is possible. We look at how your roof is built and tell you honestly what it will take, or if it is one of the few that does not suit a conversion. Neither check is a reason to worry, they are simply the sensible first steps on a newer home, and doing them upfront is what stops surprises later.

extensionTypes.title: And the older homes
extensionTypes.intro: Great Dunmow's historic core is a different picture. The Georgian and Victorian houses around the old High Street, and anything in the town's conservation area, suit a sympathetic approach, often a discreet rooflight conversion that keeps the roofline, or a carefully designed dormer where permission allows. Victorian and Edwardian houses elsewhere suit a rear or L-shaped dormer, and 1930s hipped semis a hip-to-gable. Whatever the age of your home, we match the conversion to the roof and the setting.

planning.title: Planning in Great Dunmow
paragraphs: Many Great Dunmow loft conversions are permitted development, within the volume limits (broadly 40 cubic metres for terraces, 50 for semis and detached) and the conditions, notably no dormer on the front roof slope. Mansards, front dormers and conversions in the conservation area usually need planning permission. It is worth being clear that planning permission and restrictive covenants are two separate things: planning is the council's public consent, a covenant is a private legal condition in your deeds, and a conversion can need to satisfy both. Every conversion always needs full building-regulations approval, and on a terrace or semi the Party Wall Act usually applies. We check your planning position and handle the planning, party wall and building regulations, and we flag any covenant to check so nothing catches you out.

faqs.q: Do I need to check anything beyond planning permission for a loft conversion on a modern estate?
faqs.a: Possibly, yes. Some modern developments include restrictive covenants, private legal conditions in the title deeds that are separate from planning and can affect alterations, sometimes requiring consent from the developer or a management company. They will not appear in a planning search, so it is worth checking your deeds, and asking your solicitor or conveyancer if anything is unclear. It is usually straightforward, but much better known about at the outset. We will flag it so you can check.

faqs.q: Can a relatively new house in Great Dunmow have a loft conversion?
faqs.a: Often yes, though it is usually a bigger job than on an older house. Many newer homes have trussed roofs, prefabricated frames that fill the loft with bracing, so converting them means reworking the trusses and adding structural support, normally steel. Some also have shallow roofs that limit what is possible. We look at how your roof is built and tell you honestly what it will take, and whether it suits a conversion at all.

faqs.q: What is the difference between planning permission and a restrictive covenant?
faqs.a: Planning permission is the council's public consent to carry out work, decided under planning law. A restrictive covenant is a private legal condition written into a property's deeds, which might, for example, require someone's consent before you alter the house. They are completely separate: a conversion can be permitted development, needing no planning application, and still be subject to a covenant, or vice versa. For anything to do with covenants, your deeds and your solicitor are the right sources; we simply make sure you know to check.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for a loft conversion in Great Dunmow?
faqs.a: Often not. Many hip-to-gable, dormer and rooflight conversions are permitted development within the volume limits and the front-dormer rule. Mansards, front dormers and conversions in the conservation area usually need permission. Every conversion needs full building-regulations approval. We check your position and handle whichever route applies.

faqs.q: Can my Great Dunmow loft be converted?
faqs.a: Most can. It comes down to head height (roughly 2.2 to 2.4 metres at the ridge before losing some to the new floor and ceiling), the roof structure (older cut roofs are easier than the trussed roofs on newer homes), and room for a compliant staircase. Lofts short on height can often still work with a dormer. We give you a straight answer at the site visit.

faqs.q: Do you also do extensions in Great Dunmow?
faqs.a: Yes. If a loft is not the best route, or you need ground-floor space too, we design and build extensions in Great Dunmow, see our Great Dunmow extension page. On a modern estate the same covenant checks are worth making for an extension, which we will flag, and we will advise honestly on the best route.
